title: Common CDR Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
description: The most common errors that weaken a CDR, from copied text and vague roles to missing competency mapping, with simple fixes.

data.sub: Small errors that quietly weaken a strong engineering record.

data.intro: Most weak CDRs have strong engineers behind them. The problem is how the work is presented.

sections.heading: Copied or Generic Text
paragraphs: Text taken from templates, other reports or the internet is easy to spot and can seriously harm an assessment.
sections.note: Fix: write from your own projects and keep the wording personal.

sections.heading: Describing the Team, Not You
paragraphs: Using "we" hides your contribution. The assessor wants to know what you personally designed, calculated, tested or decided.
sections.note: Fix: write in the first person and name your own tasks.

sections.heading: Vague Technical Detail
paragraphs: Statements such as "I worked on the design" prove little. Specific methods, standards, tools and results show real competence.
sections.note: Fix: state what you did, how, with which tools and what the outcome was.

sections.heading: Too Much Textbook Theory
paragraphs: Long explanations of general theory take space from your own engineering activity.
sections.note: Fix: keep theory short and spend the words on your decisions and actions.

sections.heading: Weak Competency Mapping
paragraphs: If the summary statement points to paragraphs that do not really show the element, the assessor cannot find your evidence.
sections.note: Fix: check every reference against the paragraph it points to.

sections.heading: Inconsistent Details
paragraphs: Dates, job titles and project names that differ between your résumé, episodes and CPD list raise doubts.
sections.note: Fix: build one fact sheet first and reuse it everywhere.

items.q: Can I fix a CDR that was already returned?
items.a: Yes. Read the assessor's comments carefully, address each point with real evidence and keep your facts consistent across all parts.

items.q: Is it safe to reuse a friend's CDR as a model?
items.a: Use it only to understand the structure. Copying content is risky, and your report must describe your own work.

data.heading: Spotted a few of these in your CDR?
data.text: We can fix errors and strengthen your report while keeping your real experience.
